analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign contributions at $200 per donor and bans out-of-district and PAC money.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, never received a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the money rules for House elections. It capped contributions at $200 per source, barred candidates from taking money from PACs or people outside their district, and limited candidates to $200 of their own money. It added a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 for couples) to encourage small donations, barred fundraising in the final 14 days before an election, stopped House members from running side political committees, capped leftover campaign funds at $25,000, required public disclosure of who pays for campaign ads, and barred the House from doing normal business after Labor Day in election years. It was referred to three committees on the day it was introduced and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and small donors would gain the most: a tax credit would make small contributions to House candidates half off, up to $100 per person. Challengers running against incumbents would benefit from a field where PAC money and out-of-district wealth no longer dominate. Voters would also see who is paying for campaign advertisements, because purchasers would have to publicly identify themselves and their officers before airing them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small donors, voters, and House challengers

how_it_helps.text: Caps any single source's contributions to a House candidate at $200 in total, so large donors and PACs could no longer give thousands to one member.
Bars House candidates from accepting money from PACs, individuals, or any source located outside their congressional district, keeping House campaigns tied to local voters.

Limits candidates to spending $200 of their own money, and allows an income tax credit for half of small contributions to House candidates (up to $100 per person, $200 per joint return), making it cheaper for ordinary people to support candidates.

Bans fundraising during the final 14 days before a House election, bars Representatives from running political committees beyond their main campaign committee, and caps carryover campaign funds at $25,000 between election cycles.

Requires prior public notice of the content of ads that expressly advocate a candidate's election or defeat, plus the identity of the purchaser and its officers and board members, and stops the House from conducting normal business between Labor Day and election day in election years.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, unions, corporations, and large donors would lose their ability to concentrate money on House candidates, and incumbents would lose a major fundraising edge: no more side PACs, no more unlimited war-chest carryover, and no fundraising in the last two weeks of a campaign.

drawbacks.text: A $200 cap with no full public financing system could leave House candidates short of money, and well-connected candidates might have an easier time raising many small in-district gifts than newcomers with fewer local contacts.
Barring House business after Labor Day in election years would cut roughly ten weeks of governing time every two years, allowing work only during a national emergency.

The tax credit would reduce federal tax revenue, and limits on candidate-funded and PAC money could push spending into independent advertisements, which the bill addresses only through disclosure, not limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — small, local, transparent money in House races — is broadly popular and the bill pairs limits with a small-donor tax credit, which softens the risk of starving campaigns. The weakest parts are the election-year blackout on House business and the fact that disclosure alone cannot stop independent ad spending. On balance the drawbacks are design costs, not reasons the bill's aims would fail.

outcome.mechanism: It went to three committees on the day it was introduced, a subcommittee took it up in July 1991, and it sat there with no vote of any kind until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. James T. Walsh of New York introduced the bill on May 30, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Rules committees.
Four members cosponsored the bill, two Republicans and two Democrats.
On July 12, 1991, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Rules of the House; no committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed.
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, and the bill was never considered by a committee or either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, large donors, and incumbent House members kept the existing campaign money rules, since the bill died without any vote. Ordinary voters got no change to how House campaigns are financed.

for.name: Rep. James T. Walsh
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it jointly to three committees on the day of introduction.

for.name: 4 cosponsors (2 House Republicans, 2 House Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration (and the Ways and Means and Rules committees)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 1991 to the end of the Congress without reporting it, holding any vote, or moving it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had small bipartisan sponsorship (2 of its 4 cosponsors were Republicans, 2 Democrats) but drew no votes, so the record shows no partisan split on its merits.

industries.industry: Political action committees and organized campaign donors
industries.note: The bill would bar House candidates from taking PAC money and cap every source at $200, cutting off the concentrated fundraising channel PACs rely on. Their interest lay in keeping the status quo, which ran against the bill's goal of money tied to local voters.

Groups that buy campaign ads would have to disclose the ad's content, their identity, and their officers and board members in advance. Disclosure raises their compliance burden but gives voters information about who is paying for persuasion.

Members would lose side political committees, a $25,000 cap on carried-over campaign funds, a 14-day pre-election fundraising ban, and the out-of-district money they now raise. Their interest in preserving current fundraising ran against challengers and ordinary voters.
A tax credit covering half of contributions to House candidates, up to $100 per person, would make small political giving cheaper for ordinary people.
